headline: A review of research on AI in US hospitals concludes that regulation has not kept pace with its use and names four gaps that put patient safety at risk.
score_reason: Pool 5, lowered to 4: the review was published on 14 Oct, before the window, and it is a literature review whose findings are associations.
importance_line: Patients treated with hospital AI and the clinicians who rely on it face uneven checks on whether the tools keep working and treat everyone fairly, hospitals and regulators must close the gaps, and the review draws on 22 studies, much of the evidence retrospective, so it shows associations rather than proven harm.
summary: Scienmag reports on a systematic review in Frontiers in Digital Health, led by Joseph Conteh of the University of New Mexico, which found that oversight of hospital AI is split between the FDA, the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services and others, and identified four gaps: weak monitoring after deployment, little protection against bias, unclear accountability when AI errs and limited governance capacity at hospitals. Drawing on 22 studies, the authors call for lifecycle oversight with continuous monitoring and clear responsibility, and note limits such as English-only sources and much retrospective evidence.
notes: Pool link was the Bioengineer.org copy of Scienmag's article; the Scienmag original (same slug) was read and is credited. Journal publication date 14 Oct 2026, before the window.
